docs.title: ATLAS Architecture
docs.text:
The ATLAS Cluster is build upon HW resources from old ATLAS and ABACUS clusters of DIGIS/AI and DHW centers respectively. It integrates the following types of infrastructure made available to the research units:

  • different types of GPU nodes (including V100, A40, L40, H100, H200, A5000, A6000 PRO, etc);
  • CPU nodes
  • storage infrastructure

Please note that currently the state of new unified ATLAS architecture is under development; new nodes are gradually added to the cluster. It is expected to complete the fusion of all the infrastructure by the end of 2026. See the details about migration plan and roadmap in the Migration Plan section.

The logical architecture of the ATLAS Cluster is shown in the figure below:

The architecture relies on the following building blocks:

  • Execution Platform, that takes care of running jobs, deploying supporting services and apps, run interactive workspaces. The platform relies on Kubernetes for the resource and workload management, and is extended with necessary instruments for scheduling and queueing. The execution platform is deployed on top of the HW resources of the integrated ATLAS and ABACUS cluster.
  • Persistent Data Storage implemented with S3-compatible Datalake and a relational Database (PostgreSQL) and its extensions (spatial data, vector storage). All the relevant data managed by the research units should be stored here.
  • Interactive Workspaces that allow to create and run interactive sessions (e.g., JupyterLab, VSCode). The interactive workspaces are deployed on top of the same HW resources and managed by the execution platform.
  • Management Layer (DH Core) that provides the necessary interface to launch and monitor the jobs and services in the execution platform. Together with other supporing components, the management layer forms a complete AI / MLOps platform for the development of AI applications. As such it also includes such functionality as the catalog of datasets, models and artifacts, support for experiments tracking, low-code/no-code development, etc. The interactions with the management layer may be performed through the web interface, the command line interface (CLI), or the dedicated Python SDK.

docs.title: Organization
docs.text:
The logical architecture is instantiated as a multi-tenant environment, where each research unit has a dedicated and isolated platform instance. More specifically, each tenant

  • has its own isolated storage space;
  • has its own isolated management layer;
  • manages its own interactive workspaces, services and jobs within a dedicated execution platform namespace;
  • has its own set of users corresponding to the research unit members.

The execution resources are shared between all tenants. The usage of resources is limited by the quota assigned to each tenant. See Resources and Quotas for details on how the quotas are managed, how the resources are assigned and how the jobs are scheduled within the execution platform.

When accessisng the components of the platform (either through the WEB interfaces, CLI or SDK), the users are authenticated using the FBK login credentials. The access to the datalake is based on personal session token credentials emitted by the management layer. The database storage is not available outside the cluster. The interactive workspaces are also personal and are connected to the management layer and storages automatically.

The endpoints of the tenant platform components are available through the https://*.<tenant>.atlas.fbk.eu domain, for example:

  • Management layer UI: https://core.<tenant>.atlas.fbk.eu
  • Interactive workspace manager: https://coder.<tenant>.atlas.fbk.eu

The name of the tenant corresponds to the research unit name.

Please note that the cluster is available only within the FBK network. To access the cluster outside of this network, it is necessary to access it via a VPN connection. See a dedicated FBK HowTo section on this topic.

docs.title: Functionality and Operations
docs.text: The goal of the platform is to support the development and execution of the computation intensive AI solutions and experiments, ranging from data processing and analysis to model training, to inference, and to prototyping complex ML/AI applications (e.g., RAG applications, inference services, etc). Given its functionality the platform users can perform the following operations.

docs.title: Interactive Workspaces
docs.text:
It is possible to create and run interactive sessions directly on top of the execution platform using its resources. Specifically, the users can create one or more personal interactive workspaces that are instantiated on top of the HW resources of the execution platform. Once configured and started, the users can access the interactive workspaces through the JupyterLab interface, VS Code Web interface, or from the VS Code environment on own PC using the corresponding integration support.

The interactive workspaces are automatically connected to the other components of the platform: they have the personal user credentials to access the management layer and the data storage. The users can configure the workspace resources (disk size, memory, CPU or even GPU usage), within the quotes associated to the tenant they belong to.

The workspaces may be started and stopped by the users at any time. The workspace storage is isolated and persistent. However, theno backup is performed so do not rely on it for the critical data persistence.

Note

While it is possible to assign significant resource amount to workspaces and even associate basic GPUs to it, please note that the resources are shared between all tenants and the usage is limited by the quota assigned to each tenant. See Resources and Quotas for more details.

docs.title: Computation-intensive Jobs
docs.text:
A typical and the most common scenario is to use the cluster to run research experiments that require specific hardware resources (e.g., memory, GPU, etc). As it was happening in the old cluster, such experiments are represented as a Job (represented e.g., as a Docker comtainer) that the user launches on the execution platform to perform some model training, batch processing, benchmarking, etc.

There are some significant changes with respect to the old modality of using the clusters:

  • The execution of a job is not triggered directly by the user, but is intermediated by the management layer. In fact, the users of the platform never access the HW resources directly. Instead, using the management layer it is necessary to provide the declarative specification of the executable (e.g., container to be executed) and the execution configuration, such as execution parameters/arguments, the resources to be associated, etc. The management layer will prepare the job and schedule it on the execution platform passing the necessary information. The management layer and its interfaces may be used to monitor the execution, see the execution log, resource consumption, and status.
  • Each job starts from scratch, with empty storage space. When the job completes, the resources are released and the storage is cleared. This means that, if the job uses some data or produces some output, it is responsability of the user to include the neccessary instruction to get the data (e.g., from Datalake) and to store the output upon completion (e.g., to Datalake).
  • The underlying containers are executed without root privileges. Any container with root privileges will be automatically blocked.
  • The underlying container images should be available to the cluster. It is possible to use public image registries (e.g., Docker Hub or GitHub) or to upload custom images to the cluster internal container registry.
  • Each execution is associated to a user who has requested it, and therefore to the corresponding research unit. Besides audit aspects, this information is useful for the resource utilization and budget aspects.

Note

While it is possible to run an arbitrary container in this way, the provided AI platform provides support for common types of executables, such as Python-based jobs. See thr Platform Documentation for more details.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
It is also possible to deploy and execute services on the platform. This includes, e.g., inference services, APIs, LLM models and supporting tools like embedding ranking etc. Differently from jobs, the services run and are exposed permanently, until not stopped explicitly. As in case of jobs, the same restrictions apply: non-root execution, empty ephimeral storage, etc.

Once deployed, the services are exposed within the unit namespace on a (predefined or user-specified) ports and are ready to serve the HTTP/TCP traffic.

Note

As in case of jobs, the AI platform provides support not only the possibility to deploy an arbitrary container, but also for common types of services, such as Python-based Serverless functions, LLMs compatible with OpenAI API, MLFlow model serving, etc. See thr Platform Documentation for more details.

docs.title: Data Management
docs.text:
The storage infrastructure enabled is tightly integrated with the computing nodes and allows for managing both structured and unstructured datasets. The access to the data is based on credentials managed by the management layer. The credentials are temporal and are personal; currently no permanent and/or shared credentials are supported. When working outside the platform, the credentials may be obtained with the management CLI. When working in the platform the credentials are injected automatically in the corresponding context (e.g., workspace, job, service).

While it is possible to use the persistent datastorage directly using the corresponding SDKs or tools, the management layer of the AI platform and the corresponding clients (Web, CLI, SDK) provide support for more advanced data management operations that include - Data / artifact / Model catalog - Versioning and metadata support with additional extra information (e.g., table schemas, previews, metrics, etc) - More efficient data storage - Transparent and easy to use APIs for registering, accessing, and managing the data artifacts.

docs.title: Access ATLAS tenants
docs.text:
ATLAS is a shared infrastructure, where every tenant has a dedicated, isolated namespace.

The endpoints of the tenant platform components are available through the https://*.<tenant>.atlas.fbk.eu domain, for example:

  • Main UI: https://core.<tenant>.atlas.fbk.eu
  • Interactive workspace manager: https://coder.<tenant>.atlas.fbk.eu

The name of the tenant corresponds to the research unit name.

When accessing the components of the platform (either through the WEB interfaces, CLI or SDK), the users are authenticated using the FBK login credentials via SSO.

The access to the datalake is based on personal session token credentials emitted by the management layer. The database storage is not available outside the cluster. The interactive workspaces are also personal and are connected to the management layer and storages automatically.

Warning

Please note that the cluster is available only within the FBK network.

To access the cluster outside of this network, it is necessary to access it via a VPN connection. See a dedicated FBK HowTo section on this topic.

docs.title: Run LLMs on Atlas
docs.text: Deploy an existing LLM on Atlas as an OpenAI-compatible API with DigitalHub's vllmserve-text runtime. This page explains how to choose Atlas resources and configure serving. For platform API details, see the serving section of the platform LLM tutorial (0.16.x).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Connect to your Atlas tenant from the FBK network or VPN. Use its management UI and an interactive workspace configured for that tenant.
  • Use the project setup and serving sections of the tutorial's notebook-llm.ipynb.
  • Obtain access to the chosen Hugging Face model, including approval for gated models, and create the project secret HF_TOKEN. Pass it to the service as shown in the tutorial; do not put credentials in source code or notebook cells.
  • Check your tenant's GPU availability, computational allocation, and persistent-storage quota in Resources and Quotas.

docs.title: Choose an Atlas GPU profile
docs.text:
GPU resources are not assigned by default. Select a GPU profile explicitly for the serving deployment.

The names in the Atlas profile table are display labels, not necessarily the identifiers accepted by the SDK. In your tenant's configured workspace, inspect the available profiles:

import digitalhub as dh

dh.get_k8s_resource_profiles()

Use the exact identifier returned by the API or displayed in the workload submission UI. The platform tutorial uses 1xrtxa5000-shared for serving; this is an example, not a guarantee that the same identifier or queue variant is available to your tenant. Do not derive identifiers by lowercasing the Atlas display labels or appending a queue suffix.

Atlas profile family GPUs VRAM per GPU Compute capability Maximum CPU / host RAM / ephemeral disk LLM considerations 1x5000 to 3x5000 1-3 RTX 5000 16Gi 7.5 13 cores / 39Gi / 39Gi per GPU Tight memory budget for an 8B model. FP16 weights alone take about 16 GB, leaving little room for inference overhead on one GPU; consider a smaller model or a runtime-supported quantized model. 1xA5000 to 3xA5000 1-3 RTX A5000 24Gi 8.6 13 cores / 59Gi / 59Gi per GPU More headroom for single-GPU serving, but context length and concurrency still need sizing. 1xV100 to 8xV100 1-8 Tesla V100 32Gi 7.0 10 cores / 61Gi / 61Gi per GPU More VRAM per GPU, but older architecture limits runtime and kernel compatibility; do not select solely by memory size.

The CPU, host-memory, and ephemeral-disk limits above scale with GPU count; the complete values are in Resources and Quotas. Host RAM is not GPU VRAM. Lower CPU or host-memory requests may reduce quota usage, but do not increase GPU memory or change the profile's maximum limits.

Multiple GPUs do not automatically act as one larger GPU. The model must be partitioned by a compatible runtime and configuration; selecting a multi-GPU profile alone does not enable vLLM tensor parallelism.

docs.title: Precision and runtime compatibility
docs.text:
• Use FP16 (--dtype half) rather than BF16 on the pre-Ampere RTX 5000 and V100 GPUs, subject to runtime support.
  • RTX A5000 supports newer GPU features, but the selected container, CUDA/PyTorch build, attention backend, and quantization implementation must also support the hardware.
  • Current vLLM GPU requirements specify compute capability 7.5 or higher. V100 has capability 7.0, so it is not a supported choice for current vLLM releases. Check the actual DigitalHub serving image and its version-specific requirements. Use a compatible RTX profile for the tutorial's vLLM workflow.
  • Check support for the specific model, quantization format, and attention backend, not just the minimum compute capability.

docs.title: Serve the model on Atlas
docs.text:
Use the platform tutorial's project setup and model registration steps, then create a vllmserve-text function for your existing model. For a base model without an adapter:

proj = dh.get_or_create_project("atlas-llm-serving")
base_model = proj.new_model(
    name="base-model",
    kind="huggingface",
    path="huggingface://meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B",
)
vllm_func = proj.new_function(
    name="vllm-text-serve",
    kind="vllmserve-text",
    model_name="base-model",
    url=base_model.key,
)

Replace the model identifier with the model you want to serve and can access. No adapter is required. If you already have a compatible adapter, register it and add the tutorial's adapters configuration; serving then needs both the base model and adapter.

Choose an available, runtime-compatible GPU profile and use the reserved queue for an endpoint that requires continuity. The tutorial's 1xrtxa5000-shared example is interruptible and should only be used for disposable tests that tolerate downtime.

Adapt the tutorial's vllm_func.run(...) call:

  • Set profile to the exact identifier for your selected GPU and queue.
  • Start with a shorter context, for example args=["--dtype", "half", "--gpu_memory_utilization", "0.90", "--max_model_len", "2048"], and tune after checking startup logs and memory usage. These are sizing examples, not guaranteed working values for every model.
  • Do not copy the tutorial's 32768 context length or 0.95 GPU-memory utilization blindly. Model weights, any adapter, runtime buffers, KV cache, and concurrent requests all need VRAM. Longer contexts and more simultaneous requests increase demand.
  • Keep host-memory and ephemeral-disk requests within the selected profile's limits. The tutorial's resources={"mem": "24Gi", "disk": "20Gi"} requests host RAM and ephemeral disk, not GPU VRAM. Budget disk for model downloads and staging as well.

Wait for the service to become ready, then use its platform-provided endpoint and the tutorial's OpenAI-compatible inference request. Set the request's model name to the one exposed by your deployment (base-model in the example above, or adapter when using the tutorial's registered adapter). Follow Atlas access requirements; do not assume the endpoint is publicly reachable.

docs.title: Diagnose resource problems
docs.text:
Symptom What to check Job or service remains pending Exact profile identifier, tenant allocation, queue, requested GPU type/count, CPU and host-memory requests, and current capacity. Reserved capacity does not guarantee an immediate start. CUDA out of memory Per-GPU VRAM, model precision, sequence length, batch sizes, serving context, and concurrency. A higher host-memory request does not fix GPU exhaustion. Host-memory termination or disk-full error Host RAM, ephemeral-disk limits, PVC free space, and cache/checkpoint paths. These are separate from VRAM. Unsupported GPU, dtype, or kernel error GPU compute capability and the container's CUDA, PyTorch, vLLM, quantization, and attention-backend compatibility. Workload restarts or endpoint disappears Shared-queue eviction, persistent output paths, and application-level resume support.

Consult Resources and Quotas for current limits and Troubleshooting for general Atlas issues.

docs.title: Optional: Fine-tune on Atlas
docs.text:
Fine-tuning is only needed if you want to adapt a model; it is not a prerequisite for serving. Open the tutorial notebook with its src/ directory and requirements.txt from the same branch. Use the tutorial's Python 3.11 training environment and dependencies rather than upgrading packages independently.

The tutorial's training script uses FP16 compute, eager attention, and 4-bit NF4 quantization by default. Keep those settings as the starting point on RTX 5000 and V100, and check container compatibility. The tutorial's training profile 1xrtx5000 is an example; discover the exact identifier available to your tenant. The script's device_map="auto" is not a substitute for a tested distributed-training setup.

Training with QLoRA produces an adapter, not a standalone quantized model for serving. Serving still needs the base model, and its memory footprint must be sized independently of training.

Follow the tutorial's project, secret, function creation, and image-build steps. In its training submission:

  1. Replace profile with a GPU profile available to your tenant.
  2. Start with quantization=4, train_batch_size=1, and a modest max_sequence_length (for example, 1024). These are starting points, not a guarantee that a model will fit. Size evaluation batches too.
  3. Use gradient accumulation to increase the effective batch size without increasing the per-device batch size. If CUDA runs out of memory, reduce sequence length and per-device training/evaluation batches before requesting more GPUs.
  4. Mount persistent storage at /app/local_data, as in the notebook. Set HF_HOME to /app/local_data/huggingface so model downloads use that volume.

For example, after building function_train as described in the tutorial:

TRAIN_PROFILE = "<exact GPU profile identifier from your tenant>"

train_run = function_train.run(
    action="job",
    profile=TRAIN_PROFILE,
    parameters={
        "model_id": "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B",
        "model_name": "atlas-llm-adapter",
        "hf_dataset_name": "team-bay/data-science-qa",
        "train_data_path": "DataScienceDataset.csv",
        "dev_data_path": "DataScienceDataset.csv",
        "quantization": 4,
        "train_batch_size": 1,
        "eval_batch_size": 1,
        "max_sequence_length": 1024,
    },
    secrets=["HF_TOKEN"],
    envs=[{"name": "HF_HOME", "value": "/app/local_data/huggingface"}],
    volumes=[{
        "volume_type": "persistent_volume_claim",
        "name": "atlas-llm-data",
        "mount_path": "/app/local_data",
        "spec": {"size": "50Gi"},
    }],
)

Replace the placeholder before running. The model and dataset above come from the platform example; use separate training and validation splits for a meaningful evaluation. The 50Gi volume is an illustrative starting size, not a storage requirement or an assurance of sufficient space.

docs.title: Storage and interruption constraints
docs.text:
• Budget persistent storage for the downloaded base model, datasets, Hugging Face cache, checkpoints, and final adapter/tokenizer files. A 4-bit training configuration does not mean the downloaded base-model files occupy only 4 bits per parameter.
  • The tutorial writes checkpoints under /app/local_data/checkpoints/ground and final weights under /app/local_data/weights/ground. Keep these paths on the persistent volume. Ephemeral disk is limited by the profile and is not suitable for durable outputs.
  • PVC count, PVC capacity, and S3 capacity have hard quota limits. Check available capacity before requesting a volume; GPU availability does not imply storage availability.
  • Use the reserved queue for important training runs. Shared-queue jobs may be evicted at any time. Persist checkpoints and implement and test checkpoint resume before relying on shared capacity: the tutorial calls trainer.train() without an explicit resume_from_checkpoint, so a platform restart alone does not guarantee training resumes from its last checkpoint.

docs.title: Migration and Roadmap
docs.text:
The fusion of the two clusters and the migration of the machines under the new architectural model will happen incrimentally. First, all the nodes of the old ATLAS Cluster will migrate following this schedule:

  • 21/08/2026: DGX2, RD4321
  • 18/09/2026: RF4421
  • 16/10/2026: RF4422
  • 30/10/2026: RF4423
  • 12/11/2026: RR4341

The migration of the ABACUS cluster will be completed by the end of 2026.

docs.title: Data Migration
docs.text:
When migrated, all the data on the servers will be deleted. To avoid losing the data, it is necessary to make a backup copy of the RELEVANT datasets and folders. One can use the Cloud storage options provided by FBK or use directly the Datalake of the new platform.

In the latter case it is necessary to use the corresponding S3 credentials for accessing the Datalake. If the AI platform instance is already in place for the unit, it is possible to use the personal S3 credentials. To obtain the credentials, use the management layer CLI as presented here.

As quick reference, login to the platform 

dhcli login dev-platform

and then fetch both credentials and config into a local .env file (and load with source into the current shell) 

dhcli config > dev-platform.env
dhcli credentials >> dev-platform.env
set -a && source dev-platform.env && set +a

Now you can use the environment files to configure any compatible tools like rclone or AWS CLI for this.

For example the official aws client will automatically load all config from the environment:

aws s3 sync <LOCAL_FOLDER> s3://<BUCKET_NAME>/path/to/folder

With rclone (version 1.72+ only) the only required param is --s3-env-auth=true to instruct the client in using the enviroment as source for configuration and credentials. 

rclone --s3-env-auth=true copy  --progress <LOCAL_FOLDER> ":s3:<BUCKET_NAME>/path/to/folder"

Or with the platform cli directly. In this case the uploaded files will be also registered as named entities in the catalog. 

dhcli upload -p myproject artifact -n myfolder -f folder

Alternatively, it is possible to use the functionality of the AI platform SDK for uploading the datasets and artifacts:

import digitalhub as dh

project = dh.get_or_create_project("myproject")

project.log_artifact("mydataset", kind="artifact", source="./path/to/folder/or/file/")

Note

Please take into account that the space in the datalake is not infinite; copy only really important data before the space quota runs out.

docs.title: Code Migration
docs.text:
To make the existing applications and experiments run under the new platform, it is necessary to adapt the code to the new architecture. This amounts to adding the scripts/operations to download the data before the original code and to upload the results once the code is complete (or incrementally if intermediate checkpoints should be saved as well).

When the AI platform functionality is used, it is possible for example to use the Python runtime to adapt the existing code to the new platform. See the example Pytorch project tutorial that explains the necessary steps and operations.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
In addition to the existing functionality of the platform, based on the requests from the users, more features and functionality will incrimentally be added to the platform. This includes, but not limited to,:

  • Support for Hydra-compatible jobs to spawn multiple experiment directly on the platform, without requiring intermediates like Slurm or Ray clusters.
  • Support distributed computations using Ray framework, such as for hyperparameter search or distributed training. The idea is to create the Ray clusters dynamically, based on the declarative specification, and launch the jobs on them.
  • Support for SLURM environment on top of the Kubernetes cluster of the execution platform using the corresponding Kubernetes operator.

Additional features and functionality will be added in the future. Please let us know if you have any suggestions.

docs.title: Resource Usage and Declaration
docs.text:
When launching the jobs and services, the users may declare the types and amount of resources necessary for the workload execution. The amount of resources may be specified in terms of CPU, memory, GPU or disk space. If not explicitly specified, the default values are used.

The following set of rules is used by the management layer to assign resources to the jobs and services:

  1. Workspaces. Workspace resource configuration is explicit, defining the CPU, memory and storage amount. The configuration may be changed at any time, the workspace should be restarted. The disk space, however, cannot be changed.

  2. Jobs and Services. For the jobs and services the resource declaration may be done explicity or through profilies:

  3. If no resource constraints are explicitly defined by the user, the default values are used for CPU, memory, and disk space. Specifically,

    • No GPU resources are assigned by default.
    • The default amount of memory is X Gb.
    • By default, the CPU usage is set to X core.
    • The default amount of disk space is X Gb.
  4. The user can define explicitly the requested amount of CPU, memory, and disk space. The max amount of CPU and memory is then set to 110% of that amount.
  5. To use GPUs the user should use the predefined profile defined in the cluster configuration. The profile defines the type and number of GPUs to be requested, as well as some other predefined values preconfigured according to the HW layout (e.g., memory and cores). While the profile defines the maximum amount of resources allocated to the job, the user can still define the requested amount (which is good to reduce the quota usage of the tenant).

See below the list of the currently defined profiles.

Note

The list of profiles and their characteristics is subject to change upon the migration of the cluster and changes in the HW setup.

Note

The list of profiles available to a single unit may vary. The list of the profiles available in the tenant may be obtained from the management layer using SDK or UI.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text:
Execution resources are shared across tenants, and each tenant is assigned a resource quota. The platform treats storage limits and computational resource allocations differently:

  • Hard limits cannot be exceeded. They apply to the number of Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs), PVC storage, and S3 storage. A request that would exceed one of these limits is rejected.
  • Computational allocations cover CPU, memory, GPU, and ephemeral storage. Workloads can use the tenant's allocated capacity through the reserved queue or request currently unused capacity through the shared queue.

To view the resources assigned to a tenant and its current usage, open the ATLAS monitoring dashboard. You must sign in with your FBK account.

docs.title: Workload queues
docs.text:
The platform provides two ways to run computational workloads: a reserved queue and a shared queue. Select the appropriate execution option in the workload submission interface; queue placement and resource management are handled automatically.

Warning

Every workload submitted to the shared queue is interruptible and can be evicted at any time. Use it only for workloads that can tolerate termination and restart.

docs.title: Reserved queue
docs.text:
The reserved queue uses resources allocated to the research group or project. This capacity is protected from permanent use by other groups.

  • Reserved workloads have higher scheduling priority than shared workloads.
  • If allocated resources are temporarily being used by shared workloads, the platform can reclaim them for reserved workloads.
  • This queue is appropriate for important batch workloads and workloads that should not depend on spare capacity.

Reserved capacity does not guarantee an immediate start. A workload remains pending if it requests more resources than are currently available, requires an unavailable resource type, or is waiting behind other reserved work.

docs.title: Shared queue
docs.text:
The shared queue provides opportunistic access to resources that are currently unused by their owners. It improves overall platform utilization but provides no continuity guarantee.

  • Shared workloads use spare capacity and do not own or reserve resources.
  • They have lower scheduling priority than reserved workloads.
  • Their start time depends on spare capacity being available.
  • A running shared workload can be stopped when its capacity is needed for reserved work.

After eviction, a workload may return to a pending state and restart when sufficient spare capacity becomes available. The exact restart behavior depends on the workload type and the platform abstraction used to submit it.

Shared workloads should be restartable and idempotent, persist outputs outside the running instance, and checkpoint progress when supported. Do not use the shared queue for services or jobs that require uninterrupted execution.

docs.title: Queue comparison
docs.text: Property Reserved queue Shared queue Resource source Allocated project or group resources Temporarily unused platform resources Resource ownership Allocated capacity No allocated capacity Workload priority Higher Lower Can reclaim shared capacity Yes No Interruption expectation Does not depend on spare capacity Possible at any time Recommended use Important or continuity-sensitive batch work Fault-tolerant, restartable, best-effort work

docs.title: Choosing a queue
docs.text:
Choose the reserved queue when the workload is important, has limited restart support, or needs the resources allocated to the project.

Choose the shared queue when the workload is restartable and the benefit of using additional spare resources outweighs the risk of interruption. Suitable examples include parameter sweeps, independent simulations, and jobs that save frequent checkpoints.

For shared workloads:

  • Save results and checkpoints to persistent storage, not only to the running instance's local filesystem.
  • Make processing restartable and, where possible, idempotent.
  • Split long computations into smaller independent units.
  • Do not rely on a specific start time or uninterrupted execution window.
  • Expect duplicate or partial work around an interruption and handle it safely.

docs.title: Default quotas
